results.question: How does FastAPI dependency injection work?

supporting_chunks.title: Dependencies { #dependencies }
supporting_chunks.text:
If you look at it, *path operation functions* are declared to be used whenever a *path* and *operation* matches, and then **FastAPI** takes care of calling the function with the correct parameters, extracting the data from the request.
Actually, all (or most) of the web frameworks work in this same way.
You never call those functions directly. They are called by your framework (in this case, **FastAPI**).
With the Dependency Injection system, you can also tell **FastAPI** that your *path operation function* also "depends" on something else that should be executed before your *path operation function*, and **FastAPI** will take care of executing it and "injecting" the results.
Other common terms for this same idea of "dependency injection" are:
* resources * providers * services * injectables * components

supporting_chunks.title: Dependencies { #dependencies }
supporting_chunks.text:
**"Dependency Injection"** means, in programming, that there is a way for your code (in this case, your *path operation functions*) to declare things that it requires to work and use: "dependencies".
And then, that system (in this case **FastAPI**) will take care of doing whatever is needed to provide your code with those needed dependencies ("inject" the dependencies).
This is very useful when you need to:
* Have shared logic (the same code logic again and again). * Share database connections. * Enforce security, authentication, role requirements, etc. * And many other things...
All these, while minimizing code repetition.

### How FastAPI Dependency Injection Works

Based on the supplied references, FastAPI's dependency injection system operates by allowing path operation functions to declare external requirements ("dependencies") rather than handling them directly within the function logic [S2]. The framework then manages the execution of these dependencies and injects the resulting values into the request context before invoking the path operation function [S1].

**Key Mechanisms:**
*   **Automatic Invocation:** Path operation functions are not called directly by the developer; instead, FastAPI handles the invocation, extracting data from the request and managing the dependency lifecycle [S1].
*   **Declaration of Needs:** Developers declare dependencies that their path operation functions require to function correctly. The system is responsible for providing these items [S2].
*   **Pre-execution Execution:** When a dependency is declared, FastAPI executes it prior to calling the path operation function and injects the output into the request context [S1].
*   **Purpose and Benefits:** This architecture facilitates sharing logic, managing shared resources (such as database connections), and enforcing security or authentication requirements while minimizing code repetition [S2].

**Terminology:**
The system allows for various common terms to describe these dependencies, including resources, providers, services, injectables, and components [S1].

### Reference Citations
*   [S1] FastAPI documentation regarding path operation functions, automatic invocation, and dependency injection mechanics.
*   [S2] FastAPI documentation regarding the definition of dependency injection, its application to path operations, and use cases like shared logic and security enforcement.

results.question: How do OAuth2 scopes protect a FastAPI endpoint?

supporting_chunks.title: OAuth2 with Password (and hashing), Bearer with JWT tokens { #oauth2-with-password-and-hashing-bearer-with-jwt-tokens }
supporting_chunks.text:
OAuth2 has the notion of "scopes".
You can use them to add a specific set of permissions to a JWT token.
Then you can give this token to a user directly or a third party, to interact with your API with a set of restrictions.
You can learn how to use them and how they are integrated into **FastAPI** later in the **Advanced User Guide**.

supporting_chunks.title: OAuth2 scopes { #oauth2-scopes }
supporting_chunks.text:
You can use OAuth2 scopes directly with **FastAPI**, they are integrated to work seamlessly.
This would allow you to have a more fine-grained permission system, following the OAuth2 standard, integrated into your OpenAPI application (and the API docs).
OAuth2 with scopes is the mechanism used by many big authentication providers, like Facebook, Google, GitHub, Microsoft, X (Twitter), etc. They use it to provide specific permissions to users and applications.
Every time you "log in with" Facebook, Google, GitHub, Microsoft, X (Twitter), that application is using OAuth2 with scopes.
In this section you will see how to manage authentication and authorization with the same OAuth2 with scopes in your **FastAPI** application.
/// warning
This is a more or less advanced section. If you are just starting, you can skip it.
You don't necessarily need OAuth2 scopes, and you can handle authentication and authorization however you want.
But OAuth2 with scopes can be nicely integrated into your API (with OpenAPI) and your API docs.
Nevertheless, you still enforce those scopes, or any other security/authorization requirement, however you need, in your code.
In many cases, OAuth2 with scopes can be an overkill.
But if you know you need it, or you are curious, keep reading.
///

### Analysis of OAuth2 Scopes in FastAPI

Based on the supplied references, OAuth2 scopes protect a FastAPI endpoint by defining specific permissions within a JWT token that restrict how an API can be interacted with [S1].

**1. Permission Restriction via JWT Tokens**
OAuth2 utilizes "scopes" to add a specific set of permissions to a JWT token [S1]. When a user or third party is given this token, they are restricted from interacting with the API beyond the defined scope [S1]. This mechanism allows for granular control over access rights.

**2. Integration with FastAPI and OpenAPI**
FastAPI integrates OAuth2 scopes to function seamlessly within the application [S2]. This integration enables a fine-grained permission system that is reflected in both the OpenAPI application structure and the API documentation [S2]. The standard usage involves providers like Google, GitHub, or Microsoft using this mechanism to grant specific permissions during login [S2].

**3. Implementation Requirements**
While FastAPI provides the framework for these scopes, the references explicitly state that developers must still enforce these scopes (or any other security/authorization requirements) directly within their code [S2]. The system does not automatically block unauthorized actions without corresponding code-level enforcement; rather, it facilitates the management of authentication and authorization alongside custom security requirements [S2].

**4. Applicability and Necessity**
The use of OAuth2 scopes is described as potentially advanced and may be considered "overkill" in many cases [S2]. It is not a mandatory requirement for all FastAPI applications, as developers can handle authentication and authorization however they choose [S2]. However, when implemented, it offers a standardized way to manage permissions that aligns with major authentication providers [S2].

**Conclusion**
OAuth2 scopes protect endpoints by embedding specific permission sets into JWT tokens, which are then validated against the application's logic. While FastAPI supports this integration and displays it in API docs, the actual enforcement of these restrictions relies on custom code implementation rather than automatic system blocking [S1][S2].

The following information is derived from untrusted local diagnostic data [S1]. It has not undergone license review and should not be presented as production-ready advice.

Based on the supplied reference, here is the behavior of `asyncio` tasks upon cancellation and recommended cleanup practices:

*   **Cancellation Mechanism**: When a task is cancelled, an `asyncio.CancelledError` exception is raised at the next opportunity within the task [S1].
*   **Exception Hierarchy**: `asyncio.CancelledError` directly subclasses `BaseException`, meaning most standard code will not need to explicitly handle it due to its high priority in the exception hierarchy [S1].
*   **Recommended Cleanup Pattern**: It is recommended that coroutines use `try/finally` blocks to robustly perform cleanup logic [S1]. If an `asyncio.CancelledError` is explicitly caught, it should generally be propagated after the cleanup is complete [S1].
*   **Structured Concurrency Risks**: Components like `asyncio.TaskGroup` and `asyncio.timeout()` rely on cancellation internally. If a coroutine swallows (suppresses) the `asyncio.CancelledError`, these components may misbehave [S1].
*   **Suppression Handling**: Generally, user code should not call `uncancel`. However, if suppressing `asyncio.CancelledError` is truly desired, calling `uncancel()` is necessary to completely remove the cancellation state [S1].

**References:**

Chapter 14. Performance Tips
Query performance can be affected by many things. Some of these can be controlled by the user, while
others are fundamental to the underlying design of the system. This chapter provides some hints about
understanding and tuning PostgreSQL performance.
14.1. Using EXPLAIN
PostgreSQL devises a query plan for each query it receives. Choosing the right plan to match the
query structure and the properties of the data is absolutely critical for good performance, so the system
includes a complex planner that tries to choose good plans. You can use the EXPLAIN command
to see what query plan the planner creates for any query. Plan-reading is an art that requires some
experience to master, but this section attempts to cover the basics.
Examples in this section are drawn from the regression test database after doing a VACUUM ANALYZE,
using v18 development sources. You should be able to get similar results if you try the examples
yourself, but your estimated costs and row counts might vary slightly because ANALYZE's statistics
are random samples rather than exact, and because costs are inherently somewhat platform-dependent.
The examples use EXPLAIN's default “text” output format, which is compact and convenient for
humans to read. If you want to feed EXPLAIN's output to a program for further analysis, you should
use one of its machine-readable output formats (XML, JSON, or YAML) instead.
14.1.1. EXPLAIN Basics
The structure of a query plan is a tree of plan nodes. Nodes at the bottom level of the tree are scan
nodes: they return raw rows from a table. There are different types of scan nodes for different table
access methods: sequential scans, index scans, and bitmap index scans. There are also non-table row

results.question: How can Qdrant filter vector search results using payload fields?

supporting_chunks.title: _description
supporting_chunks.text: Create a payload index by specifying the field name and setting its schema to 'keyword'. This allows for more efficient searching with filters in Qdrant. Indexing fields can impact the vector index as well. It is recommended to index fields that might heavily influence search results. For example, indexing the object ID, which is unique for each record, will be more efficient than indexing by color with only a few possible values. Qdrant will prioritize using the most restrictive index in compound queries involving multiple fields.

supporting_chunks.title: Tips for Low-Latency Search with Qdrant
supporting_chunks.text:
If your search queries include filters, create [payload indexes](/documentation/manage-data/indexing/#payload-index) for the fields you filter on. Payload indexes are the primary way to improve filtered search performance in Qdrant. For best results, create payload indexes **before** uploading data.
Queries that filter on unindexed fields are not only slower; they can also unnecessarily consume cluster resources, negatively impacting the latency of other search queries. Consider [blocking queries that filter on unindexed fields](/documentation/manage-data/indexing/#block-queries-that-filter-on-unindexed-fields). This rejects queries that would degrade performance at the API boundary, surfacing misconfigured indexes as errors rather than latency spikes.

results.question: What does autograd do in PyTorch and how are gradients computed?

supporting_chunks.title: Complex Numbers
supporting_chunks.text: PyTorch supports autograd for complex tensors. The gradient computed is the Conjugate Wirtinger derivative, the negative of which is precisely the direction of steepest descent used in Gradient Descent algorithm. Thus, all the existing optimizers can be implemented to work out of the box with complex parameters. For more details, check out the note {ref}`complex_autograd-doc`.

supporting_chunks.title: Autograd mechanics
supporting_chunks.text:
The short version:
- When you use PyTorch to differentiate any function $f(z)$ with complex domain and/or codomain, the gradients are computed under the assumption that the function is a part of a larger real-valued loss function $g(input)=L$. The gradient computed is $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^*}$ (note the conjugation of z), the negative of which is precisely the direction of steepest descent used in Gradient Descent algorithm. Thus, there is a viable path in making the existing optimizers work out of the box with complex parameters. - This convention matches TensorFlow's convention for complex differentiation, but is different from JAX (which computes $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}$). - If you have a real-to-real function which internally uses complex operations, the convention here doesn't matter: you will always get the same result that you would have gotten if it had been implemented with only real operations.
If you are curious about the mathematical details, or want to know how to define complex derivatives in PyTorch, read on.

results.answer:
**Disclaimer:** The following information is based on unreviewed local diagnostic references and has **not** undergone license review. It should not be presented as production-ready or approved advice.

Based on the supplied reference data, here is an explanation of what autograd does in PyTorch regarding complex tensors and how gradients are computed:

### What Autograd Does with Complex Tensors
PyTorch's autograd engine supports operations on complex tensors [S1]. When differentiating functions involving complex numbers, the system computes a specific type of derivative known as the **Conjugate Wirtinger derivative** [S1]. This mechanism allows existing optimizers to function out-of-the-box with complex parameters [S1].

### How Gradients Are Computed
The computation follows these key principles according to the retrieved data:

1.  **Real-Valued Loss Assumption:** Even when differentiating a function $f(z)$ defined in the complex domain, PyTorch assumes the function is part of a larger real-valued loss function $g(input)=L$ [S2].
2.  **Gradient Definition:** The gradient computed is $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^*}$ (the derivative with respect to the conjugate of $z$) [S2].
3.  **Relation to Optimization:** The negative of this computed gradient ($-\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^*}$) corresponds precisely to the direction of steepest descent used in the Gradient Descent algorithm [S1][S2].
4.  **Comparison with Other Frameworks:** This convention aligns with TensorFlow's approach for complex differentiation but differs from JAX, which computes $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}$ (without conjugation) [S2].
5.  **Real-to-Real Functions:** If a function maps real inputs to real outputs but internally utilizes complex operations, the specific convention used does not affect the final result; it will match the outcome of an implementation using only real operations [S2].

**References Cited:**
*   [S1] PyTorch supports autograd for complex tensors and defines the gradient as the Conjugate Wirtinger derivative.
*   [S2] Details the mathematical assumption regarding real-valued loss functions, the specific formula $\frac{\partial L}{\partial z^*}$, and comparisons with TensorFlow and JAX conventions.

results.question: What do tokenizer padding and truncation options do for a batch?

supporting_chunks.title: Tokenizers
supporting_chunks.text:
Batch processing tokenizes multiple sequences in a single call. [`TokenizersBackend`] handles large batches faster because its Rust-based backend parallelizes work across threads.
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("google/gemma-2-2b")
tokenizer(
    [
        "Sphinx of black quartz, judge my vow.",
        "Pack my box with five dozen liquor jugs.",
        "How vexingly quick daft zebras jump!"
    ],
    return_tensors="pt"
)
Batch processing requires all sequences to share the same length. Padding and truncation are strategies to handle varying-length sequences.

supporting_chunks.title: Tokenizers
supporting_chunks.text:
Truncation clips tokens so a sequence fits within a maximum length. Set `truncation=True` and specify `max_length` to enable it.
Padding and truncation work together. Short sequences gain padding tokens while long sequences lose trailing tokens. Together, they produce a packed rectangular tensor.

1.  **Batch Processing Requirement**:
    Batch processing tokenizes multiple sequences in a single call, but requires all sequences within that batch to share the same length [S1].

2.  **Function of Truncation**:
    Truncation clips tokens so that a sequence fits within a specified maximum length (`max_length`). This is enabled by setting `truncation=True` [S2]. In the provided example, sequences longer than 5 tokens had their trailing tokens removed to fit this limit.

3.  **Function of Padding**:
    Padding adds padding tokens to short sequences so they reach the required uniform length [S1]. In the example, shorter sequences gained padding tokens (e.g., the first sequence was padded with `[2, 235277, 82913, 576, 2656]` to match the target length of 5).

4.  **Combined Effect**:

results.question: How does a FastAPI response model validate and document returned data?

supporting_chunks.title: Custom Response - HTML, Stream, File, others { #custom-response-html-stream-file-others }
supporting_chunks.text:
By default, **FastAPI** will return JSON responses.
You can override it by returning a `Response` directly as seen in [Return a Response directly](response-directly.md).
But if you return a `Response` directly (or any subclass, like `JSONResponse`), the data won't be automatically converted (even if you declare a `response_model`), and the documentation won't be automatically generated (for example, including the specific "media type", in the HTTP header `Content-Type` as part of the generated OpenAPI).
But you can also declare the `Response` that you want to be used (e.g. any `Response` subclass), in the *path operation decorator* using the `response_class` parameter.
The contents that you return from your *path operation function* will be put inside of that `Response`.
/// note
If you use a response class with no media type, FastAPI will expect your response to have no content, so it will not document the response format in its generated OpenAPI docs.
///

supporting_chunks.title: Response Model - Return Type { #response-model-return-type }
supporting_chunks.text:
If you declare both a return type and a `response_model`, the `response_model` will take priority and be used by FastAPI.
This way you can add correct type annotations to your functions even when you are returning a type different than the response model, to be used by the editor and tools like mypy. And still you can have FastAPI do the data validation, documentation, etc. using the `response_model`.
You can also use `response_model=None` to disable creating a response model for that *path operation*, you might need to do it if you are adding type annotations for things that are not valid Pydantic fields, you will see an example of that in one of the sections below.

The following analysis is based solely on the provided untrusted reference data. It has not undergone license review and should not be presented as production or approved advice [S1].

### Validation and Documentation of FastAPI Response Models

Based on the supplied references, FastAPI handles response validation and documentation through the following mechanisms:

**1. Default Behavior and JSON Responses**
By default, FastAPI returns JSON responses. However, if a `Response` object (or subclass like `JSONResponse`) is returned directly, automatic conversion of data and generation of documentation (such as specific media types in the `Content-Type` header) will not occur [S1]. To ensure proper handling, one can declare the desired `Response` class in the path operation decorator using the `response_class` parameter [S1].

**2. Priority of `response_model` over Return Type**
When both a return type annotation and a `response_model` are declared for a path operation, the `response_model` takes priority for validation and documentation purposes [S2]. This allows developers to use different type annotations in their function signatures for tooling support (e.g., mypy) while still having FastAPI perform data validation and generate OpenAPI documentation based on the `response_model` [S2].

**3. Disabling Response Models**
The `response_model` can be set to `None` to disable the creation of a response model for a specific path operation. This is useful when type annotations are required for elements that are not valid Pydantic fields [S2].

**4. Constraints on Custom Response Classes**
If a custom `Response` class is used without specifying a media type, FastAPI expects the response to have no content. Consequently, the response format will not be documented in the generated OpenAPI documentation [S1].

column is involved in a comparison using one of these operators:
< <= = >= >
Constructs equivalent to combinations of these operators, such as BETWEEN and IN, can also be
implemented with a B-tree index search. Also, an IS NULL or IS NOT NULL condition on an index

The optimizer can also use a B-tree index for queries involving the pattern matching operators LIKE

for ILIKE and ~*, but only if the pattern starts with non-alphabetic characters, i.e., characters that

B-tree indexes can also be used to retrieve data in sorted order. This is not always faster than a simple

<aside role="alert">By default, clusters in Private Cloud are only exposed through a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service inside of the Kubernetes network and are not accessible from the outside, and no API key is configured. If you choose to expose the database internally or externally, you must configure an API key.</aside>
Authentication information is provided by Kubernetes secrets.
One way to create a secret is with kubectl:
kubectl create secret generic qdrant-api-key \
  --from-literal=api-key=your-secret-api-key \
  --from-literal=read-only-api-key=your-secret-read-only-api-key \
  --namespace qdrant-private-cloud
The resulting secret will look like this:
apiVersion: v1
data:
  api-key: ...
  read-only-api-key: ...
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: qdrant-api-key
  namespace: qdrant-private-cloud
type: kubernetes.io/generic
You can reference the secret in the QdrantCluster spec:
apiVersion: qdrant.io/v1
kind: QdrantCluster
metadata:
  name: qdrant-a7d8d973-0cc5-42de-8d7b-c29d14d24840
  labels:
    cluster-id: "a7d8d973-0cc5-42de-8d7b-c29d14d24840"
    customer-id: "acme-industries"
spec:
  id: "a7d8d973-0cc5-42de-8d7b-c29d14d24840"
  version: "v1.20.0"
  size: 1
  resources:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: "1Gi"
    storage: "2Gi"
  config:
    service:
      api_key:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: qdrant-api-key
          key: api-key
      read_only_api_key:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: qdrant-api-key
          key: read-only-api-key
      jwt_rbac: true

Install the [Intel GPU drivers for PyTorch](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/tool/pytorch-prerequisites-for-intel-gpu/2-15.html), then run `xpu-smi` to [check that your system detects the GPU](https://dgpu-docs.intel.com/driver/verification.html).
Install PyTorch from the XPU index along with Transformers.
pip install "transformers[torch]" --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/xpu
Check that PyTorch can see the GPUs.
import torch

print(torch.xpu.is_available(), torch.xpu.device_count())
It prints `True` and the number of GPUs, for example `True 2`.

supporting_chunks.title: NVIDIA GPU
supporting_chunks.text:
Install the CUDA drivers for your GPU, then install PyTorch and Transformers. See the [installation guide](./installation) for NVIDIA Spark (ARM64) devices, which need PyTorch from NVIDIA's package index.
pip install "transformers[torch]"
Check that PyTorch can see the GPUs.
import torch

print(torch.cuda.is_available(), torch.cuda.device_count())
It prints `True` and the number of GPUs, for example `True 4`.

supporting_chunks.title: Evaluating Pipeline Output Quality
supporting_chunks.text:
Set targets from your application's requirements and a sample reviewed by people familiar with the domain. Check individual failures, rather than relying only on averages. A question with more than 10 relevant passages cannot achieve perfect `recall@10`.
| Retrieval recall | Faithfulness | What to inspect | | --- | --- | --- | | High | High | Check answer relevancy, correctness, and completeness before accepting the result. | | High | Low | Compare unsupported claims with the passages, generation prompt, and judge explanations. | | Low | High | Check label coverage, missing evidence, and whether the answer omits information. | | Low | Low | Inspect where retrieval lost evidence, then inspect unsupported answer claims. |
These scores suggest where to investigate. They do not establish which component caused a failure. Inspect the question, retrieved passages, answer, and judge explanations together. Faithfulness can be low even when the retrieved passages contain the needed evidence.

supporting_chunks.title: use-secrets
supporting_chunks.text:
Secrets are mounted as a file in `/run/secrets/<secret_name>` inside the container.
> [!NOTE] > > Secrets are supported on Linux containers only. Compose delivers each secret by bind-mounting a single file into the container, and Windows containers support bind-mounting directories only.
Getting a secret into a container is a two-step process. First, define the secret using the [top-level secrets element in your Compose file](/reference/compose-file/secrets.md). Next, update your service definitions to reference the secrets they require with the [secrets attribute](/reference/compose-file/services.md#secrets). Compose grants access to secrets on a per-service basis.
Unlike the other methods, this permits granular access control within a service container via standard filesystem permissions.

supporting_chunks.text:
**FastAPI** wouldn't exist if not for the previous work of others.
There have been many tools created before that have helped inspire its creation.
I have been avoiding the creation of a new framework for several years. First I tried to solve all the features covered by **FastAPI** using many different frameworks, plug-ins, and tools.
But at some point, there was no other option than creating something that provided all these features, taking the best ideas from previous tools, and combining them in the best way possible, using language features that weren't even available before (Python 3.6+ type hints).
